messages.subject: SEM with quadratic interrelationships
messages.subject_clean: SEM with quadratic interrelationships
messages.body_plain:
Hello lavaan comunity,

SEM are completely new to me, so please excuse any possible gaps. I want to compare the profile variability ( Var(y)) of three groups and I am faced with various problems.

We have the estimations of the y-parameters and we assume in accordance to Bohrnstedt & Goldberger (1969) that they result to:

Var(y) ≈ [E²(yc) + E²(ys) + Var(yc) + Var(ys)] + [E²(yE1) + E²( yE2) +  E²( yE3)  + Var( yE1) +  Var( yE2 + Var( yE3) ]

We assume, that the profile variability can decomposed to the variance of a consistent [E²(yc) + E²(ys) + Var(yc) + Var(ys)] and an inconsistent part   [E²(yE1) + E²( yE2) +  E²( yE3)  + Var( yE1) +  Var( yE2 + Var( yE3) ] .

Is it possible, to make an appropriate modell with lavaan? If so, I would be very grateful for any advice on how to build the model. I think there's a problem, because of the quadratic interrelationships. Can anybody help me? Any help would be appreciated.

messages.subject: "Standard" Chi-Square for WLSMV
messages.subject_clean: "Standard" Chi-Square for WLSMV
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am running an analysis that compares a number of approaches to handling non-normality.  I am finding that the WLSMV chi-square under the "Standard" column is very much lower than the robust column and also very much lower than the same column for MLR.  For example, the standard chi-square for MLR is 770.994 compared to 168.287.  Similarly, for WLS the standard chi-square is 690.2 compared to 168.287 for the WLSMV standard chi-square.  I'm not sure I have seen such large differences.  Any thoughts?

Thanks!

messages.subject_clean: NPD warning
messages.body_plain:
My first guess would be scaling of common factors. You set first loadings for fac1_17, fac2_17 and fac4_17 to be "NA"--that is, to be free parameters--and you specified std.lv <http://std.lv>=F, so you are not standardizing your common factors. You must either constrain loadings or fix factor variances (OK, or use the effects coding option), or a factor model is not identified. I believe, if you remove the NA modifiers, or remove the std.lv <http://std.lv>=F option, the model will be identified.

messages.subject: Parameter estimates, CIs and p-values inconsistent across unstandardized and standardized solutions
messages.subject_clean: Parameter estimates, CIs and p-values inconsistent across unstandardized and standardized solutions
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am
running a cross-lagged model to study the relationships between anxiety and
social communication over two time points. I have noticed that when I get parameter
estimates and confidence intervals for the unstandardized solution, these are very
different to the parameter estimates and confidence intervals for the
standardized solution.

I am using
the following line of code to get confidence intervals for the unstandardized parameter
estimates:

·
summary(fit,
ci = TRUE)

And this line
of code to get confidence intervals for the standardized parameter estimates:

·
standardizedSolution(fit,
ci = TRUE, level = 0.95)

When I do this, one of my model's pathways is significant when I look at the unstandardized parameter estimate (b
= .019, 95% CIs [.004, .035], p = .015), but non-significant when I look at the standardized one (β =
.185, 95% CIs [-.791, 1.160], p = .710).

Any information
on why this may be the case, or advice on how to interpret this discrepancy,
would be much appreciated.

Thank you,

Elise

messages.subject: Re: Importing a model from dagitty
messages.subject_clean: Importing a model from dagitty
messages.body_plain:
Here's what worked for me, in case it's helpful to anyone else.

"dag" is the name of the dagitty object generated by the daggity function in the daggity package; "df " is the name of the dataframe where variables that are used in the DAG are either real or (if endogenous) ordered. Unused variables in the dataframe are ok.

The loop adds all the directed paths and covariances to a lavaan syntax string, except for covariances that involve an exogenous variable (discerned from the DAG) and/or an ordered variable (discerned from the data).

lavsyntax <- ''
for (i in (1:nrow(edges(dag)))) {
  lavline <- ifelse(edges(dag)[i,"e"] == "->",
                    paste(edges(dag)[i,"w"], "~", edges(dag)[i,"v"]),
                    ifelse(edges(dag)[i,"v"] %in% exogenousVariables(dag)|edges(dag)[i,"w"] %in% exogenousVariables(dag)|is.ordered(df[edges(dag)[i,"w"]])|is.ordered(df[edges(dag)[i,"w"]]),
                           "",
                           paste(edges(dag)[i,"w"], "~~", edges(dag)[i,"v"])))
  lavsyntax <- paste(lavsyntax, lavline, sep = " \n ")
}

Pat

Hi Pat

Thanks for the syntax. I don't know if I can contribute anything useful. I will give it a try. Would this simplify the code a bit?

lavsyntax <- function(obj) {
  res <- apply(edges(obj), 1, function(x) {
    op <- switch(x["e"], "->" = "~", "<->" = "~~")
    c(x["w"], op, x["v"], "\n")
  })
  paste(res, collapse = "")
}
lavsyntax(dag)

I didn't understand exactly what is being done with the DF. But it seems like if a certain condition is present, no lavaan syntax line should be created? Would that be an alternative solution then?

lavsyntax <- function(obj) {
  res <- apply(edges(obj), 1, function(x) {
    op <- switch(x["e"], "->" = "~", "<->" = "~~")
    cond <- if(edges(dag)[i,"v"] %in% exogenousVariables(dag)|edges(dag)[i,"w"] %in% exogenousVariables(dag)|is.ordered(df[edges(dag)[i,"w"]])|is.ordered(df[edges(dag)[i,"w"]]) TRUE else FALSE
    if(cond) c(x["w"], op, x["v"], "\n")
  })
  paste(res, collapse = "")
}

Best

Christian

Von: 'Pat Malone' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
Gesendet: Freitag, 4. März 2022 16:50
An: lav...@googlegroups.com <lav...@googlegroups.com>
Betreff: Re: Importing a model from dagitty

Here's what worked for me, in case it's helpful to anyone else.

"dag" is the name of the dagitty object generated by the daggity function in the daggity package; "df " is the name of the dataframe where variables that are used in the DAG are either real or (if endogenous) ordered. Unused variables in the dataframe are ok.

The loop adds all the directed paths and covariances to a lavaan syntax string, except for covariances that involve an exogenous variable (discerned from the DAG) and/or an ordered variable (discerned from the data).

lavsyntax <- ''
for (i in (1:nrow(edges(dag)))) {
  lavline <- ifelse(edges(dag)[i,"e"] == "->",
                    paste(edges(dag)[i,"w"], "~", edges(dag)[i,"v"]),
                    ifelse(edges(dag)[i,"v"] %in% exogenousVariables(dag)|edges(dag)[i,"w"] %in% exogenousVariables(dag)|is.ordered(df[edges(dag)[i,"w"]])|is.ordered(df[edges(dag)[i,"w"]]),
                           "",
                           paste(edges(dag)[i,"w"], "~~", edges(dag)[i,"v"])))
  lavsyntax <- paste(lavsyntax, lavline, sep = " \n ")
}

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Just to close the loop on this thread.. I'm just posting this response below from Yves (with my questions interspersed) in case it's useful for others / in the future

>
>         On 2/22/22 12:44, Laura Havers wrote:
>          > Just to check my understanding in that case, does this mean
>         that the
>          > standard errors (and test statistic, I believe) are only
>         adjusted where
>          > there is clustering *within groups (and that there is no need
>         for
>          > correction where there is clustering *across groups)?
>
>         Hm. If you have both groups and clusters, then the groups must
>         be on the
>         highest level. For example, students in (a random sample of)
>         schools, in
>         two countries. Here, countries would be the group variable, and
>         school
>         the cluster variable.
>
>         As soon as the cluster sizes are larger than 1, we need to
>         'correct' for
>         the clustering.
>
>         It is in general not possible to have groups within clusters. An
>         example
>         would be male and female students in schools. We could have
>         'gender' as
>         a covariate in a multilevel SEM, but we can not treat 'gender' as a
>         'group' in a multigroup analysis. The reason is that the latter
>         requires
>         that the groups are independent.
>
>          > I'm puzzled though... I previously ran some measurement
>         invariance
>          > models using the same specification (i.e., group = random,
>         cluster =
>          > family), and the models ran without error (I know this
>         because I have
>          > the results!). Am I going completely mad, or might there have
>         been an
>          > update or something similar to lavaan over the past year or
>         so that
>          > could have previously allowed the models to run?
>
>         That could be. I do not remember when this 'check' has been
>         introduced,
>         but it is very likely that it was not there (yet) in the early
>         releases
>         of the 0.6 series.
>
>         In any case, the (older) results should be very similar to what
>         you get
>         if you omit the cluster= argument altogether. Assuming there is
>         only a
>         single observation in each cluster.
>
>         Yves.
>
>         --

On Thursday, 17 February 2022 at 17:25:05 UTC yros...@gmail.com wrote:
> On 2/14/22 16:26, Laura Havers wrote:
> > Error in lav_data_cluster_patterns(Y = X[[g]], clus = clus, cluster =
> > cluster,  :
> >   lavaan ERROR: everything cluster contains only one observation.
>
> The error message (where 'everything' should be 'every', will fix that)
> indicates that each cluster has only 1 observation.
>
> > model_22 <-
> >   'p22 =~ p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + p5 + p6 + p7 + p8 + p9 + p10 + p11 + p12
> > + p13 + p14 + p15'
> > fit_model_22 <- cfa(model_22, data=data, group = "random", cluster =
> > "famID", estimator = "MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv>=F, missing = "fiml")
> > summary(fit_model_22, fit.measures=T, standardized=T)
>
> > N = 13555, with two family members per family (so two rows /
> > participants have the same value for "famID").
>
> What is the "random" variable? I think you need to remove the group =
> "random" altogether.
>
> As you seem to have two family members only, you may consider reshaping
> your data in 'wide format', so that the variables of the two family
> members are in the same row, and the rows become the families.
>
> See: https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1689366
>
> This paper is mostly about categorical data, but it works equally well
> with continuous data.
>
> Yves.

Dear Community,

Lavaan newbie here.  I've been trying to specify a latent growth curve model as per attached path diagram in R for a few days now. The theoretical path is reasonably clear to me, however I am failing to translate my theoretical ideas (as in the path diagram) into a working lavaan code.
I would like to build such a model for each of a total of 15 personality traits. Each personality trait was collected at three measurement times with 4 items each. Also, I would like to add age and gender as covariates, stepwise I would also like to add age^2 and age^3 to see if these effects are more fitting.
Attached is my path diagram for an exemplary personality trait.

This is what my code (exemplary for one personality trait) looks like so far, but unfortunately I get very poor fits, sometimes even negative degrees of freedom.

lgcmAengst <- '
i =~ 1*T1NeuroAengstlichkeitMean + 1*T2NeuroAengstlichkeitMean + 1*T3NeuroAengstlichkeitMean
s =~ 0*T1NeuroAengstlichkeitMean + 1*T2NeuroAengstlichkeitMean + 2*T3NeuroAengstlichkeitMean

i ~ SQ1_age + SQ1_sex
s ~ SQ1_age + SQ1_sex '

lgcmAengstfit <- growth(lgcmAengst, data = daten)
summary(lgcmAengstfit, fit.measures=TRUE)

Does anyone have any ideas where errors could be?

Thanks so much in advance.
Thorben

PS: TXNeuroAengstlichkeitMean is the mean value out of the 4 items that have been collected at the measurement point for this trait.

messages.subject: Re: partial and semipartial correlation interpretation
messages.subject_clean: partial and semipartial correlation interpretation
messages.body_plain:
> standardized regression coefficient ... equivalent to the partial correlation

No, they are related but have different denominators.  Unstandardized multiple-regression slopes are indeed partial regression slopes, and standardized slopes are interpreted the same way, but in units of the variables' total SD:

> interpreted as the standard deviation unit change in intent that results from a one standard deviation unit change in attitudes. Right?

Correct.  Partial correlations are expressed in residual (not total) SD units.  Semipartial is a mix (residual SD of partialed variables, total SD of unpartialed variables)

> I can get the total R2 of the model fairly easily using the rsquare=T option in summary, but I could use some help on how to get semipartial correlations using ppcor and how to interpret them in context of SEM?

If you calculate the change in R-squared between 2 nested models, the semipartial correlation is the square-root.  Just as the partial correlation is the square-root of partial eta/R-squared.  Why can't you just pass your data to the ppcor package?  If the data are/include latent variables, then you can save the correlation matrix using lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>") or lavInspect(fit, "cor.all") and pass the relevant submatrix to ppcor (but then you couldn't trust any statistical tests, because they are estimates, not observed data).

> Also, how would I get the proportion of variance in intent explained by each factor?

If the predictors are correlated, their explained variance will overlap.  Squaring the relevant partial correlation (using ppcor, see above) will give you partial eta/R-squared per predictor.

messages.subject: Re: (Residual) Variances Interpretation
messages.subject_clean: (Residual) Variances Interpretation
messages.body_plain:
> Why does the Variance section for my model does not have p values for the observed variables?

Because those are not estimated parameters (by default) when the observed variables are categorical.

http://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

> Can I display the variances of the observed variables in the path diagrams along with the variances for latent variables, even though I do not know if the variances for the observed variables are significant or not.

Yes.  Most people have no hypotheses about the residual variances, so a hypothesis test is irrelevant.

> What is the difference in the interpretations of the unstandardized v/s standardized variances. (Like for the covariance section, the estimates (unstandardized) are covariances, whereas the standardized ones showcase the correlation between factors/latent variables). For all the observed variables the unstandardized and standardized values are the same, but they are different for the latent variables which have p values with them.

The "std.all" solution rescales such that everything is in units of SD, rather than the original units of the variables.  For categorical data, the units of the latent responses are arbitrary anyway (see linked paper above), and are identical under the default parameterization="delta" when setting std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE.

> I will be reporting the standardized values in the path diagram so if anyone could kindly tell me its interpretation.

1 minus the standardized solution's residual variance is R-squared.  Standardizing an exogenous variance just sets it to 1, nothing to interpret.

messages.subject: Re: Exogenous variable effect coded (-1 / 1) possible in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Exogenous variable effect coded (-1 / 1) possible in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
> Now I am wondering, will Lavaan create wrong estimates if I used my experimental conditions as IV that are coded as -1 / 1?

Define "wrong".  If you are comparing your results to a regression model that controls for Country using dummy/effects codes, the estimates will differ from a multigroup SEM that estimates an intercept for each Country.  The same could be done in a regression model that excludes the (fixed) intercept, so that each Country's dummy code is included (i.e., no reference group).  But then each other predictor's effect would need to be moderated by Country as well, unless you are equating them across groups in the SEM.

> running the same model with dummy coded variables for y1 and y2 gives me different estimates

Because a 1-unit difference does not mean the same thing for a dummy code (treatment vs. control) as for an effect code (treatment vs. average of treatment/control groups).  If you want the same 1-unit effect, you could use effect codes -0.5 and +0.5.

messages.subject: Re: "Standard" Chi-Square for WLSMV
messages.subject_clean: "Standard" Chi-Square for WLSMV
messages.body_plain:
> standard chi-square for MLR is 770.994 compared to 168.287.  Similarly, for WLS the standard chi-square is 690.2 compared to 168.287 for the WLSMV standard chi-square.  I'm not sure I have seen such large differences.  Any thoughts?

For MLR (Huber-White / sandwich-style scaling factor) , the discrepancy (quantified by the scaling factor) depends on the levels of the kurtosis because the standard chi-squared is scaled using fourth-order moments.  A recent pub describes how to derive expected moments (1-4) for normal data discretized by given thresholds:  https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2021.1988609
I expect there should be an analytical solution to derive the scaling factor, too.  But I expect it is informative enough to simply check the univariate kurtosis of your descriptives, e.g., using psych::describe()

For DWLS with a scaled and shifted statistic, I think the scale and shift parameters depend on the amount of uncertainty when estimating the thresholds and polychoric correlations.  Although not adjusted for nonnormality per se, they should be indirectly dependent on the nonnormality of the discrete observations.  For example, I would expect that highly skewed discrete observations must have fewer observations in extreme categories, which makes those thresholds less certain, and thus polychorics involving such variables less certain.  Thus, I expect highly skewed discrete observations to also have more extreme scale/shift parameters.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Why Not Bootstrap
messages.subject_clean: Why Not Bootstrap
messages.body_plain:
> Bootstrapping is used when the data is not normal.

May I know why you think so?

> However, in AMOS when we need to assess mediation, we have to check direct and indirect effects.

I think you meant checking the check boxes to ask for the direct and indirect effects in the output. I am not sure what you meant by "However". In lavaan, we also need to tell lavaan we want to estimate indirect effect. We even need to form the product of path coefficients ourselves. AMOS enumerates all possible indirect effects automatically. In this aspect, AMOS is more convenient.

Nevertheless, AMOS does *not* estimate indirect effects along some paths automatically (e.g., in a parallel mediation model); we need to form the parameters ourselves:

http://amosdevelopment.com/features/user-defined/user-defined-simple/Tutorial2/pdf/SimpleUserDefined2.pdf

This is quite inconvenient. It is much easier to specify the indirect effects to estimate in lavaan if we are interested in individual pathways.

> However, in Lavaan, we do not need to bootstrap (although we can) for indirect effects.

The indirect effect in SEM is a user-defined parameter (e.g., the product of two path coefficients). By default, lavaan uses the delta-method to form the CIs for user-defined parameters, including the indirect effect. Do you imply that delta-method CI is better than bootstrapping CI for an indirect effect?

As far as I know, AMOS cannot produce delta-method CI for user-defined parameters (I may be wrong because there are a lot of functions in AMOS that I am not familiar with). In lavaan, we can request delta-method CI (default) or bootstrapping CI. I think it is a question of which CI is better rather than which program is better for estimating an indirect effect. The default method may or may not be the best method.

I hope I did not misunderstand your question.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am planning a bivariate LGCM analysis and in order to know which models will be (over)identified and thereby usable for nested model comparisons, I have calculated degrees of freedom (unique elements - free parameters) by hand.

To double-check, I then ran the planned model on some other data in lavaan, and the degrees of freedom is not consistent with what I had previously calculated...!

The model is straight-forward, six observed variables, three for each set of growth factors, resulting in two (linear: 0, 1, 2) slope factors and two intercept factors, where I allow covariances among all growth factors. Intercepts of the observed I have fixed to zero, based on the default in the growth() function and general recommendations. See below for how I write out the model.

According to my calculations the number of free parameters for the model is 20, which lavaan agrees with. Number of unique elements I have calculated as (K*(K+1))/2 = 6*(6+1)/2 =  6*7/2 = 42/2 = 21. Subtracting 20 (for free parameters) from 21 should therefore give 1 degree of freedom.

However, in the lavaan output, df for the Used Defined Model is 7 (see output below). I'm clearly missing something here! Some guidance here would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks!

Jonna

*** model formulation ***
lin_bivar <-  '

# latent
i_pre =~ 1*P1_log + 1*P2_log + 1*P3_log
S_pre =~ 0*P1_log + 1*P2_log + 2*P3_log
i_post =~ 1*P4_log + 1*P5_log + 1*P6_log
S_post =~ 0*P4_log + 1*P5_log + 2*P6_log

# intercepts
i_pre ~ 1
S_pre ~ 1
i_post ~ 1
S_post ~ 1  #intercepts for latent var are estimated

P1_log ~ 1*0
P2_log ~ 1*0
P3_log ~ 1*0
P4_log ~ 1*0
P5_log ~ 1*0
P6_log ~ 1*0  #intercepts for observed var fixed to zero

# variances
i_pre ~~ i_pre
S_pre ~~ S_pre
i_post ~~ i_post
S_post ~~ S_post
P1_log ~~ P1_log
P2_log ~~ P2_log
P3_log ~~ P3_log
P4_log ~~ P4_log
P5_log ~~ P5_log
P6_log ~~ P6_log #variances are estimated for latent and observed

# covariances
i_pre ~~ S_pre
i_post ~~ S_post
i_pre ~~ i_post
S_pre ~~ S_post
i_pre ~~ S_post
i_post ~~ S_pre #all covariances among latent variables are estimated
'
f_lin_biv <-lavaan(lin_bivar, data=bdnf, estimator='ml', missing="FIML")
summary(f_lin_biv, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE, ci=TRUE)

messages.subject: Re-scaling / transforming factor loadings
messages.subject_clean: Re-scaling / transforming factor loadings
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to replicate the CFA for ipsative items as suggested by Cheung & Chan (2002). Their model imposes a 'rescaling parameter' on the factor loadings (see p. 66). In the proposed model, each factor loading is 'rescaled' by subtracting the average value for all factor loadings. Roughly reproducing their proposal, a one-factor model with three observed indicators such as

factor1 =~ load1*x1 + load2*x2 + load3*x3

would be transformed to

factor1 =~ tran1*x1 + tran2*x2 + tran3*x3

where
tran1 = load1 - ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)
tran2 = load2 - ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)
tran3 = load3 - ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)

I wonder how this transformation of factor loadings could be implemented in lavaan. (Other proposed transformations seem to be more easily implemented in lavaan.)

Thanks!

Mike W.-L. Cheung & Wai Chan (2002) Reducing Uniform Response Bias With Ipsative Measurement in Multiple-Group Confirmatory Factor Analysis, Structural Equation Modeling, 9:1, 55-77.
https://doi.org/10.1207/S15328007SEM0901_4

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jasper,

Thank you very much for your response.

I believe the warning is due to the data. I have tried to change the optimization method from the default NLMINB to BFGS, and it says that there are negative latent variable variances, especially for the factor 'Att.' When I tried to double-check with a PCA and scree plot, I got the data to load to three factors (and not four). I have tested other models (i.e., three-factor and unidimensional), and the data fit (albeit mixed/poorly) these two different models. I would like to believe that the Heywood case/ negative lv variances are due to structural misspecification, or in other words, the bifactor solution is not feasible.

I would like to hear your views if my reasoning could be considered a possibility.

Thank you.

Best,

Esau

Hi Esau,

I am hesitant to give concrete advise as I am not very experienced and because I do not have a clear answer to your problem. Nonetheless, here are some thoughts I have:

1) Have you considered performing explorative factor analysis to make sure you find a correct factor structure?
2) Do you use the orthogonal = TRUE option (in the cfa function) intentional?
3) You mentioned that (some of) the items are not normally distributed, maybe you could try using the satorra bentler correction and a scaled test statistic?

I hope these thoughts may help you find a solution.

Best wishes,

Jasper Bogaert

messages.subject: Re: Using categorical data in lavaan (vs. STATA)
messages.subject_clean: Using categorical data in lavaan (vs. STATA)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If you have categorical endogenous variables, you can indeed just use ordered = TRUE if all the items are categorical. If not all the items are categorical, you can specify those items that are categorical in the ordered option (instead of using TRUE). If you do this, then the WLSMV estimator will be used by default. I found this information in the lavaan tutorial (https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html):

"If all the (endogenous) variables are to be treated as categorical, you can use ordered = TRUE as a shortcut.

When the ordered= argument is used, lavaan will automatically switch to the WLSMV estimator: it will use diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) to estimate the model parameters, but it will use the full weight matrix to compute robust standard errors, and a mean- and variance-adjusted test statistic. Other options are unweighted least squares (ULSMV), or pairwise maximum likelihood (PML). Full information maximum likelihood is currently not supported."
It looks equivalent to the gsem command in STATA to me. However, I have not much experience with STATA so I am not 100% sure. I hope we can get confirmation from someone else.

Best wishes,

Jasper Bogaert

PhD student and teaching assistant
Department of Data Analysis (PP01)
Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences
Ghent University

On Sunday, March 13, 2022 at 10:57:27 AM UTC+2 jasper.b...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi,
>
> If you have categorical endogenous variables, you can indeed just use ordered = TRUE if all the items are categorical. If not all the items are categorical, you can specify those items that are categorical in the ordered option (instead of using TRUE). If you do this, then the WLSMV estimator will be used by default. I found this information in the lavaan tutorial (https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html):
>
> "If all the (endogenous) variables are to be treated as categorical, you can use ordered = TRUE as a shortcut.
>
> When the ordered= argument is used, lavaan will automatically switch to the WLSMV estimator: it will use diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) to estimate the model parameters, but it will use the full weight matrix to compute robust standard errors, and a mean- and variance-adjusted test statistic. Other options are unweighted least squares (ULSMV), or pairwise maximum likelihood (PML). Full information maximum likelihood is currently not supported."
> It looks equivalent to the gsem command in STATA to me. However, I have not much experience with STATA so I am not 100% sure. I hope we can get confirmation from someone else.
>
> Best wishes,

messages.body_plain:
Hello again!

It seems like I had not included the mean structure in counting the unique pieces of information. A variance-covariance matrix of 21 plus 6 means gives 27 unique pieces of information. And 27 - 20 free parameters gives 7 degrees of freedom.

Problem solved, I think!

Jonna

messages.subject: Re: Re-scaling / transforming factor loadings
messages.subject_clean: Re-scaling / transforming factor loadings
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christian,

This transformation has been proposed by Cheung & Chan to address some measurement issues with ipsative data. The transformation/correction basically states that a said loading must be 'corrected' taking the average of all loadings in consideration. E
quality of loadings (e.g., load1 = load2 = load3) is not required.

I just added a print screen of the model proposed by Cheung & Chen for clarification -- I hope there is no copyright issues with that.

The factor loadings transformation is what I have found challenging to implement. I am unsure about how to define the transformation using lavaan syntax. Cheung & Chan provide EQS syntax in the appendix but I haven' t used EQS in ages so I am unable to convert it into lavaan syntax.

Best,
Fabricio

On Friday, March 11, 2022 at 5:55:57 PM UTC christia...@hhl.de wrote:
> Hi Fabricio,
>
> I do not know this transformation. What I wonder is this:
>
>
> tran1 = load1 - ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)
> tran2 = load2 - ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)
> tran3 = load3 - ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)
>
> means
>
> load1 = ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)
> load2 = ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)
> load3 = ((load1 + load2 + load3)/3)
>
> This should only be the case if load1 = load2 = load3. Right?
>
> Maybe I'm making a big error in reasoning (it's already late in the evening) or the transformation works somehow differently? Or is it an additional parameter calculated based on the estimated loadings (in which case it would be easy)?
>
> Best
>
> Christian
>
> Von: lav...@googlegroups.com <lav...@googlegroups.com> im Auftrag von Fabrício Fialho <fabrici...@gmail.com>
> Gesendet: Freitag, 11. März 2022 18:01
> An: lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
> Betreff: Re-scaling / transforming factor loadings
>
> Hi all,
>
> I am trying to replicate the CFA for ipsative items as suggested by Cheung & Chan (2002). Their model imposes a 'rescaling parameter' on the factor loadings (see p. 66). In the proposed model, each factor loading is 'rescaled' by subtracting the average value for all factor loadings. Roughly reproducing their proposal, a one-factor model with three observed indicators such as
>
> factor1 =~ load1*x1 + load2*x2 + load3*x3
>
> would be transformed to
>
> factor1 =~ tran1*x1 + tran2*x2 + tran3*x3
>
> where

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Not an academic here, and not a whole lot of experience with SEM.
Just trying to do a practical application of CFA after doing EFA and forcing loadings for a work project, and trying to understand implications of these warning messages I'm getting

If I get warning messages:
'lavaan WARNING: Model estimation FAILED! Returning starting values'
'lavaan WARNING: estimation of the baseline model failed.'

Are these a big deal? I'm trying to do fit.measures=TRUE in my summary and it also tells me 'lavaan WARNING:  fit measures not available if model did not converge' - I'm guessing this is to do with my earlier model failure?

For additional context...
I'm doing a very large CFA, testing 30 factors/latent variables, each with 345 variables (very initial iterations, will chop and change this). As this is very large, I've written my equations in a .txt file and used R's readLines function on it. My dataset contains 317k rows, and I'm doing this in local memory. I've tested this on a 100-row subset of the data and I still get the same warnings from earlier

Any help at all is appreciated! Let me know if you'd like any further detail

Thanks,
Allan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alan,

The errors are a big deal, especially in this case because the model did not converge, or in other words, no solution has been found. By consequence, you will not have fit measures (or any other results). It seems like you have a very complex and large model. This requires a lot of data. Could you try running the analysis again with a much larger subset of the data? Am I correct to assume that 100-row subset of the data is the same as using 100 observations? In that case you do not have enough data in your subset.

If it would still not work with much more data, you might want to have another look at your model (or the EFA). If that does not help you could also try to use regSEM to make your model a bit smaller. These are just some thought that popped up, hope it helps!

Best wishes,

Jasper Bogaert

Ghent University

messages.body_plain:
I am a total beginner to both SEM and R, so some of the things I ask about might be weird, sorry about that! Here is my issue:

I am using runMI for a path analysis, as I have a good deal of missing data in a mixed dataset (=not able to use fiml), and for several reasons I am using 20 imputed datasets (using mice - using amelia still leaves me with my issue). Using the built in imputation in runMI would not solve my issue either (see below).

For the imputation to go through correctly, variable classes need to be specified correctly (factors or numeric).The imputations work well, but now I am faced with the issue of using categorical data in lavaan.
if I understand this <https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html> correctly, lavaan allows for binary and ordinal variables, albeit in different forms for endogenous and exogenous variables. I have one binary endo variable, and that can be specified in an argument in the runMI command (and I have done so (ordered = "myVar"), seems to work fine). I have three exogenous variables that are ordered. For them to work in the model, I would have to respecify them as numeric. HOWEVER, since these are tied up in a list of 20 imputed datasets, I have not found a way to force them to be numeric AFTER imputation (has to be afterward, or the imputation will not be performed correctly). Therefore, lavaan returns an error, notifying me of the factors that need to be dealt with.

I realize this might not be a specific lavaan issue - if there is some way to respecify the variables post-imputation then there is no problem. Is there anything I can do?

messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I am trying to get the results of my sem model which uses a dataset that is multiple imputed. I have had no success with this. when I declare `fit.measures = TRUE` in the summary function, I get the below error. Does anybody have a solution for this?

I have downloaded the latest versions of lavaan and semTools, despite this, the issue still persists. See below for a reproducible code and sessioninfo.

Error in .local(object, ...) : unused argument (fit.measures = TRUE)

# download pacman package if not installed, otherwise load it
if(!require(pacman)) install.packages(pacman)

# loads relevant packages using the pacman package
pacman::p_load(
  dplyr,
  semTools,
  lavaan,
  mice )

# make 10 dataset using mice

boys_imp <- boys %>%
  mice(.,
       m = 3,
       cluster.seed = 1234)

# set up model
fit <-  "sem =~ age + bmi + hc + hgt + wgt"

# run model
model_fit <- semTools::cfa.mi(fit,
                              fun = "sem",
                              miPackage = "mice",
                              parallel = "snow",
                              ncpus = 7,
                              seed = 9862,
                              estimator = "MLM",
                              std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
                              data = boys_imp)

# summarise model
summary(model_fit,
        test = "D2",
        pool.robust = TRUE,
        ci = TRUE,
        fit.measures = TRUE,
        standardized = TRUE
)

messages.subject: Change in Degrees of Freedom (ML vs DWLS)
messages.subject_clean: Change in Degrees of Freedom (ML vs DWLS)
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan community,

I simulated the following model:

pop.model <- '
# measurement model
    fac1 =~  1.2*x3 + 0.5*x4
    fac2 =~  1.2*x5 + 0.5*x6 + 0.3*x7
    fac3 =~  0.8*x8 + 0.7*x9 + 0.6*x10

# structural model
     y ~ 0.2*x0 + 0.5*x1 + 0.6*x2 + 1.5*fac1 + 2*fac2 + 0.5*fac3
'
set.seed(1234)
N <- 400
dataset <- simulateData(pop.model,  sample.nobs = N)

After that I estimate the follwing model

model.user <- '    fac1 =~ x3 + x4
                              fac2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7
                              fac3 =~ x8 + x9 + x10

                               y ~ x0 + x1 + x2 + fac1 + fac2 + fac3
'

sem.model <- sem(model, data = dataset.3.3)
summary(sem.model, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

The degrees of freedom in the summary output are 63 (baseline) and 46 (user). I tried to calculate the degrees of freedom in the follwing way

ov <- dim(dataset)[2] # number of observed variables
fp <- dim(parameterEstimates(sem.model.user.3.3, remove.nonfree = TRUE))[1] # number of free parameters to be estimated
ov_sm <- 3 # number of observed exogenous variables in the regression
df_null <- ov*(ov+1)/2 - ov - ov_sm*(ov_sm-1)/2
df_user <- ov*(ov+1)/2 - ov_sm*(ov_sm-1)/2 - fp - ov_sm
c(df_null, df_user)
# 63, 46

I get the same degrees of freedom as in the summary of lavaan. In the next step  I recoded the observed endogenous variable "y" the follwing way

dataset$ycat <- cut(dataset$y, breaks = 5, labels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5"))

and get now a categorical observed endogenous variable "ycat" with 5 levels. After that I estimate the follwing model

model.ord <- '                fac1 =~ x3 + x4
                                        fac2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7
                                        fac3 =~ x8 + x9 + x10

                                        ycat ~ x0 + x1 + x2 + fac1 + fac2 + fac3
'

sem.model.ord <- sem(model.ord, data = dataset, ordered = "ycat")

where I specify that "ycat" is a ordered categorical variable. Lavaan now use the DWLS estimator instead of the ML estimator.

summary(sem.model.ord, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

Running the summary function I get now 36 (baseline) and 46 (user) degrees of freedom. Does it make sense that the degrees of freedom of the baseline model are smaller than the degrees of freedom of the user model, the more complex model? I thought the degrees of freedom should decrease by 5, because of the addtional estimated thresholds for "ycat".

Has anyone an explanation for this? Where this difference in degrees of freedom between ML and DWLS comes from?

I am very grateful for any tip.
Simon

messages.body_plain:
Hi Allan,

I took a look at your model and the subset of the data. I see two problems:

First of all your model is too big (but you already mentioned this yourself). I would suggest refining your research problem and/or question of interest and only use the variables needed. If you struggle with this I would suggest using some form of regularization to obtain a more parsimonious model with only most interesting factors and items.

A second issue could be the data itself. I only have a subset of your data, but it does not look normally distributed. One of the assumptions is that the items are normally distributed. If this is not the case, you may want to use the satorra-bentler correction (it is an option in the cfa and/or sem function).

These are just suggestions, I hope they can help you a bit further.

It might also be worth waiting for someone else to jump in or to have another look.

Best wishes,

Jasper

messages.body_plain:
Hello Lavaan community,

I am trying to conduct an EFA of 19 survey questions and trying to remove variance due to cross-classified repeated measures/conditions (repeated observations from participants for the same question with different contexts). Even if I restrict the model to just one cluster, I get the following error message:

Error in this.label.set %in% LABEL.group1 :
  object 'LABEL.group1' not found

The model runs perfectly fine without clusters, and Lavaan can recognize the clusters if I treat them as groups for a multiple-group approach. I cannot find any information online about what the above error message means. Any ideas as to what the problem might be? Please see below my code and attached my data for reference.

#CoW EFA 1-factor code
CoW_f1 <- '
#CoW  EFA factor #1
efa("efa")*CoW_f1 =~ q1 + q2 + q3 + q4 + q5 + q6 + q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
'
#CoW EFA 1-factor code MULTILEVEL
CoW_f1 <- '
#CoW 1-factor EFA
level: 1
efa("efa")*CoW_f1 =~ q1 + q2 + q3 + q4 + q5 + q6 + q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
level: 2
q1 ~~ q1 + q2 + q3 + q4 + q5 + q6 + q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q2 ~~ q2 + q3 + q4 + q5 + q6 + q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q3 ~~ q3 + q4 + q5 + q6 + q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q4 ~~ q4 + q5 + q6 + q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q5 ~~ q5 + q6 + q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q6 ~~ q6 + q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q7 ~~ q7 + q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q8 ~~ q8 + q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q9 ~~ q9 + q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q10 ~~ q10 + q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q11 ~~ q11 + q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q12 ~~ q12 + q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q13 ~~ q13 + q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q14 ~~ q14 + q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q15 ~~ q15 + q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q16 ~~ q16 + q17 + q18 + q19
q17 ~~ q17 + q18 + q19
q18 ~~ q18 + q19
q19 ~~ q19
'
library(lavaan)
library(semTools)

CoW_f1_run <- sem(
  model          = CoW_f1,
  data           =subset(GPP_Study_9A_IntDat_long_q_wide, SurveyLength == "Long"),
  auto.efa       = T,
  #group = "primary_character",
  std.lv <http://std.lv> = T,
  parameterization = "theta",
  ordered = c("q1","q2","q3","q4","q5","q6","q7","q8","q9","q10","q11","q12","q13","q14","q15","q16","q17","q18","q19"),
  missing = "pairwise",
  estimator = "WLSMV",
  rotation = "oblimin",
  #group = "secondary_character"
  cluster = "IntDat_IDs" #c("primary_character","secondary_character") #IntDat_IDs
)

summary(CoW_f1_run, fit.measures=T)

Hi Artem,

Here is the entire code I used. At the very bottom, I run lavTestScore(fit.scalar) and View(parTable(fit.scalar)) to determine parameters to release.

Hope that helps,
Kindly,
Brandon

cfs_efa_model_001 <- '
factor2 =~ Q1_8 + Q2_2 + Q3_2 + Q4_2 + Q5_2
factor4 =~ Q2_4 + Q3_4 + Q4_4 + Q6_4
factor6 =~ Q1_6 + Q2_6 + Q3_6 + Q4_6
Q4_4 ~~ Q6_4
'

######
######
######
# INVARIANCE TESTING
######
######
######

# add grouping variable here
g1 <- "dissgroup"
# add factor model here
mft_fact <- cfs_efa_model_001
# add data variable here
mft_dat <- cfs_3middle

#Invariance testing
syntax.config <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data=mft_dat, parameterization="theta",
                               ID.fac="std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4))
cat(as.character(syntax.config))
summary(syntax.config)
## threshold invariance
syntax.thresh <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4), group.equal = "thresholds")
## notice that constraining 4 thresholds allows intercepts and residual
## variances to be freely estimated in all but the first group & occasion
cat(as.character(syntax.thresh))
## print a summary of model features
summary(syntax.thresh)
## Fit a model to the data either in a subsequent step:
mod.config <- as.character(syntax.config)
fit.config <- cfa(mod.config, data = mft_dat, group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                  parameterization = "theta")

lavInspect(fit.config, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

## or in a single step:
fit.thresh <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                            parameterization = "theta",
                            ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                            group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4), group.equal = "thresholds", return.fit = TRUE)
## compare their fit to test threshold invariance
anova(fit.config, fit.thresh)

######
# METRIC INVARIANCE TESTING
######

## metric invariance
syntax.metric <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                               group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings"))
summary(syntax.metric)                    # summarize model features
mod.metric <- as.character(syntax.metric) # save as text
cat(mod.metric)                           # print/view lavaan syntax
## fit model to data
fit.metric <- cfa(mod.metric, data = mft_dat, group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                  parameterization = "theta")
## test equivalence of loadings, given equivalence of thresholds
anova(fit.thresh, fit.metric)

######
# SCALAR INVARIANCE TESTING
######

## scalar invariance
syntax.scalar <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                               group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings",
                                               "intercepts"),
                               group.partial = c("Q2_4 ~1","Q3_4 ~ 1", "Q3_2 ~ 1"))
summary(syntax.scalar)                    # summarize model features
mod.scalar <- as.character(syntax.scalar) # save as text
cat(mod.scalar)                           # print/view lavaan syntax
## fit model to data
fit.scalar <- cfa(mod.scalar, data = mft_dat, group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                  parameterization = "theta")
## test equivalence of intercepts, given equal thresholds & loadings
anova(fit.metric, fit.scalar)

######
# INVARIANCE TESTING TABLE
######

## For a single table with all results, you can pass the models to
## summarize to the compareFit() function
compareFit(fit.config, fit.thresh, fit.metric, fit.scalar)

lavInspect(fit.metric, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

#TEST FOR which parameters to release
lavTestScore(fit.scalar)

View(parTable(fit.scalar))

messages.body_plain:
Dear community,

I would like to ask for your help regarding a SEM analysis that I am conducting in Lavaan.

It is a mediation model with 2 independent variables, one mediator and one outcome variable. I started by fitting the measurement model, and then switched to the structural model. The result is that both models  (measurement and structural) are identical: the fit indices are exactly the same (chisq = 116.7, df = 70, CFI = .966, TLI = .956, RMSEA = .057, SRMR = .070).

I seems very unlikely to me that this happened  by chance.  Does anyone know what this means, and how I should interpret this?

Thank you very much for your help!

Alice

messages.subject: Re: Measurement model and structural model having exactly same fit indices
messages.subject_clean: Measurement model and structural model having exactly same fit indices
messages.body_plain:
Is this what the structural part of your model is?

mediator ~ iv1 + iv2
outcome ~ mediator + iv1 + iv2

"iv1 ~~ iv2" not explicitly included but should be there by default in lavaan.

If this is your structural model, then what you found is expected. This model is saturated at the structural level, with respect to the variance-covariance matrix of the latent factors. You cannot empirically differentiate the structural model and the measurement model.

-- Shu Fai

Behavioural intention is predicted by performanceexpectancy, Effortexpectancy, etc.
Behavioural intention ~ performanceexpectancy + Effortexpectancy + ... + ...

Fran

messages.subject: Re: TIME FOR EXECUTING lavTestScore
messages.subject_clean: TIME FOR EXECUTING lavTestScore
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I have a 5 factor/23 indicator multi-group CFA model (7 groups), which I believe is configurally and metrically invariant. It is however not scalar invariant, so I am trying to understand if it can be made to be partially scalar invariant by freeing some parameters. I am using lavTestScore() to do this, but having attempted twice to run this, it takes well over 3 hours, and then RStudio terminates. Are there any other methods I can use to discover which constraints could be freed in order to achieve partial scalar invariance?

Thanks so much
Victoria

On Saturday, July 10, 2021 at 1:12:30 PM UTC+1 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Scalar invariance does not hold.
>
> You cannot conclude that without first constraining thresholds to equality.  Your loadings are not comparable if the scales of the latent response variables are not linked (by equating thresholds).  Try using semTools::measEq.syntax(), and reading the references on that help page.
>
>
> > I'm trying to run lavTestScore ... It began two days ago
>
> That should not happen.  It should only take moments.
>
> > Is there any way to calculate it in advance?
>
> In advance of what?  It is calculated from the first and second derivatives of the estimated model parameters, so you need to estimate a model first.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject: FIT indices behave as if model is saturated, why?
messages.subject_clean: FIT indices behave as if model is saturated, why?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to understand why  the fit indices of my model behave like a saturated model when I still have a degree of freedom. I have some ideas as to why (below) but it is unclear to me if these are correct. I am also struggling with interpretation and would like some guidance.

For context on my results:
I have a model with one degree of freedom and a very large N (~10.000).
My robust RMSEA is 0.000, robust CI's [0.000, 0.017]. My CFI and TLI are 1.
These are the values associated with my chi-square:

For the RMSEA at least, I can intuit that my chi-square is just smaller than my degrees of freedom (which is 1) and so it defaults to zero as the denominator in the sqrt((x^2-df)/(df(N-1)) formula for computing RMSEA is negative. I assume something similar is happening with the CFI and TLI.  Is this correct?

Additionally, it is unclear to me how I should interpret these results. Technically my model is not saturated right? But is it the case that all models where X^2 is smaller than the DFs behave (in their fit indices) like a saturated model?

Finally, I assume the x^2 is small because there is little discrepancy between observed and modelled data, as X^2 is just ~F(N-1) where F should be the maximum likelihood discrepancy between my observed and implied data/var-covar matrices. Additionally this X^2 is non-significant. So:

1) I assume this means that there is good agreement between my model and my data.
2) But, aren't these results saying my model is overfitting the data? and sorry for the silly question but: can you overfit even when your model is not saturated?
3) Are there circumstances without overfit  where you could get  RMSEA=0, CFI/TLI=1?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: FIT indices behave as if model is saturated, why?
messages.subject_clean: FIT indices behave as if model is saturated, why?
messages.body_plain:
The formulas for RMSEA and CFI are such that, if chi-square < df, then RMSEA = 0 and CFI = 1.
With 1 df, your data does not disagree with your model, but it has a very limited range to disagree. Especially if the model was specified with an eye to fit, it may be better to say that the model does not disagree with the data used to specify the model, which will not be a surprise.
There is no way to assess "overfit" from the information provided. Your model may be an insightful depiction of a complex system or it may be that the constraints that give rise to your 1 df are trivial and not of interest.

messages.subject: Summer workshops on SEM and Panel Models in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Summer workshops on SEM and Panel Models in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am teaching a 12-hour introductory SEM course on July 4-6, as well as an 8-hour introduction to panel models on July 7-8.  It will be taught in person this year, but it is also possible to attend remotely.  They will be taught in the morning in Barcelona, Spain, so the time will unfortunately not be convenient to attend remotely from the Americas or eastern Australia.

I will of course use lavaan for instruction.  As you can read in the course descriptions linked below, the approach is quite practical.  The SEM topics will not be advanced, but they may still be of value to members of this group. Indeed, I would be very specific about which constraints you want to test, so that those are the only calculations that occur. You can't.  You are using all the available information to estimate those parameters.  You can still interpret the parameters, but your structural hypotheses couldn't possibly be disconfirmed by the data.  A more restrictive hypothesized structure (e.g., full mediation) would buy you df.

messages.subject: reproduce growth model (FIML estimation) with covariance matrices
messages.subject_clean: reproduce growth model (FIML estimation) with covariance matrices
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've fitted a multivariate latent growth curve model and, since there are NAs, FIML estimation (fit). Now I would like to reproduce the model without raw data, i.e. only with the covariance matrices, means, etc (fit2). You can find my code below (I am not allowed to share the raw data, regrettably).

There are some differences in the outputs. In particular, the latent means are estimated to be zero in fit2.  I guess I am missing something.  Also, I do not get the robust statistics (apparently "mlr" is not allowed).

Is there a way to reproduce the model perfectly in lavaan without raw data (i.e., no discrepancies in the output)?

Thank you!
Giovanni

##### CODE #####

## Model ----

model <- paste0(
  c(

    paste0("i_VIQ =~ ", paste0(rep(1, 8), "*", # intercept_VIQ
                               paste0("VIQ", 1:8), collapse = " + ")),
    paste0("i_PIQ =~ ", paste0(rep(1, 8), "*", # intercept_PIQ
                               paste0("PIQ", 1:8), collapse = " + ")),

    paste0("s_VIQ =~ ", paste0(round(c(0.000000, 1.000000, 1.460722, 2.304858, 2.853997, 3.229938, 3.571941, 3.607097), 3), "*", # pre-defined slope lambdas
                               paste0("VIQ", 1:8), collapse = " + ")), # slope_VIQ
    paste0("s_PIQ =~ ", paste0(round(c(0.000000, 1.000000, 1.104614, 1.927702, 3.288916, 4.267016, 5.285423, 7.610444), 3), "*", # pre-defined slope lambdas
                               paste0("PIQ", 1:8), collapse = " + ")), # slope_PIQ

    paste0(c(
      "s_VIQ ~~ s_PIQ", "i_VIQ ~~ i_PIQ",
      "s_VIQ ~~ i_VIQ", "s_PIQ ~~ i_PIQ",
      "s_VIQ ~ 1", "i_VIQ ~ 1",
      "s_PIQ ~ 1", "i_PIQ ~ 1"),
      collapse = "\n"),

    # residual variances

    paste0(paste0("VIQ", 1:8), " ~~ u_VIQ*", paste0("VIQ", 1:8), collapse = "\n"),
    paste0(paste0("PIQ", 1:8), " ~~ u_PIQ*", paste0("PIQ", 1:8), collapse = "\n"),

    # regressions

    "s_VIQ ~ i_PIQ + cov1 + cov2 + cov3",
    "s_PIQ ~ i_VIQ + cov1 + cov2 + cov3",

    "i_VIQ ~ cov1 + cov2 + cov3",
    "i_PIQ ~ cov1 + cov2 + cov3",

    "\n"),

  collapse = "\n")

## Fitting the models ----

fit <- growth(model, data = df, # model with raw data containing NAs
  missing = "fiml", estimator = "mlr")

cov <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov
mean <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat")$mean
N <- lavInspect(fit, "nobs")
WLS.V <- lavInspect(fit, "WLS.V")
NACOV <- lavInspect(fit, "gamma") # NULL

fit2 <- growth(model, sample.cov = cov, sample.nobs = N,
            WLS.V = WLS.V, NACOV = NACOV)

summary(fit, fit.measures = T, standardized = T)
summary(fit2, fit.measures = T, standardized = T) # different results

messages.subject_clean: Standardised coefficients being equal to standardised ones
messages.body_plain:
> Aren't the z-values provided automatically by the lavaan output a standardised solution as well?

That "standardizes" the estimate by its SE, not the SDs of the predictor and outcome.

> Why do we report lavaan's "standardized" solutions, such as the ones in the std.all column as opposed to the z-values?

As an effect size, like reporting standardized slopes for a regression model.

> Can the z-value of an indirect effect be considered the effect size of that effect?

No, it is a (Wald z) test statistic, influenced by N, as opposed to a standardized effect size (independent of N).

> > the standardised solutions (shown in the table at the bottom) are the same the unstandardised ones. This is the same case with my data.

> > ...

> > Does this have to do with having had standardised all my data (by passing it by the "scale" function in R) before fitting the model?

Yes, if your SDs are already 1, then the solution is already in units of SD.

FYI, you cannot trust your p values when you do that.  You can obtain p values for the standardized estimates from standardizedSolution().

messages.body_plain:
> I am attaching a text file with my code and data

Thanks.  I tried running the model on the first imputation, which produces that warning about correlations near 1 of x3 with x5 and with x6.  Indeed, I see that lavCor() shows correlations no higher than .65, but that is returning unconditional correlations.  The default setting with categorical data is conditional.x=TRUE, which estimates residual correlations after partialing out exogenous covariates.  When I look at your estimates for the first imputation, I can see a big problem:

fit1 <- sem(paths_1, data = impList[[1]], ordered = "x3")
lavInspect(fit1, "est")$psi
        x4      x3      x5      x6
x4   4.060
x3   0.000   1.000
x5   0.000   0.000   0.834
x6   0.000   0.000 -26.229   0.830

Beyond the out-of-bounds residual covariance (partial correlation = -31.521), neither x3 nor x4 are correlated with x5 or x6 after x1, x2, and the 3 covariates are partialed out.   That would rule out your mediation hypothesis, but of course this result is suspect because the x5-x6 correlation is impossibly large.

When I tried fitting the model without first partialing out exogenous effects, other warnings appear:

fit1 <- sem(paths_1, data = impList[[1]], ordered = "x3", conditional.x = FALSE)
Warning messages:
1: In muthen1984(Data = X[[g]], wt = WT[[g]], ov.names = ov.names[[g]],  :
  lavaan WARNING: trouble constructing W matrix; used generalized inverse for A11 submatrix
2: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= -4.133521e-19) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that
    the model is not identified.

I think you might not have enough data to support estimating this model.  Or this might simply be consistent with the result above: That there are no correlations to model after accounting for the covariates, which causes estimation problems when you try.  When only 20 of 92 observed x3 values are in one category, it is not likely that the combination of predictors (nearly) completely accounts for those individual differences.

As a last resort, I even tried setting all your exogenous variables as.numeric in the original data to use estimator="PML" with pairwise deletion, while treating only x3 as categorical.

fit1 <- sem(paths_1, data = data_rep, ordered = "x3",
            estimator = "PML", missing = "pairwise",
            fixed.x = FALSE, conditional.x = FALSE)

This yielded a result, but neither of the mediators have significant effects (also problems with the model fit stats).  Rather than trying to get this to work in the most ideal way, I would consider whether the obtainable results make it seem unreasonable to pursue this mediation model further, at least until/unless more data can be gathered.  I say that while being completely naive about the nature or stakes of your study, so salt is needed.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: No scalar (full or partial) equivalence in evidence - what next?!
messages.subject_clean: No scalar (full or partial) equivalence in evidence - what next?!
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Have been toiling over a SEM for close to three months for a masters thesis, and admittedly, I have made it rather complicated (using WLSMV estimation on World Values Survey data, having different levels for the indicators, some are 9, some are 10, some are 4)!

My model is 7 countries (as the group indicator) with 5 latent variables representing 23 indicators. I have not been able to use lavtestscore except by using it in a piecemeal fashion (so releasing 10 parameters at a time, and there are around 1900, so you can imagine how time-consuming this has been!) so have taken to omitting an item one-by-one and then returning to configural, then metric, then scalar testing, in an effort to prove partial scalar invariance.

Every time, I get really good results on configural and metric, but a big degradation when moving to scalar testing. (So config > CFI.scaled = 0.945; RMSEA.scale = 0.072, then metric > CFI.scaled = 0.941; RMSEA.scaled = 0.072, but then scalar > CFI.scaled = 0.867; RMSEA.scaled = 0.087).

As I said, I can't just run lavTestScore() on the whole scalar model as it won't converge, and running it a bit at a time is not practical, so I don't know where to go from here. I am happy to state in my thesis that the MGCFA is configural and metric invariant, but evidence for scalar invariance is lacking. But I want to then regress these latent factors on a dependent variable, and of course without scalar invariance, I fear that is not a sound approach. Would it therefore be reasonable to create 7 separate SEMs (one per country)?

Thanks.

messages.subject_clean: Fixing factor loading to 1: different results depending on choice
messages.body_plain:
The standardized solution and the model-implied moments (thus, the fit statistic) are scale invariant.  However, unstandardized estimates are entirely dependent on the arbitrary scale assigned to the common factor(s), so different indicators lead to different results.  Loadings will be proportionally equivalent regardless of which is fixed to 1, but unfortunately, their SEs (and therefore Wald z tests) are not proportionally equivalent.  Because some indicators are more reliable than others, fixing different ones results in different imprecision of estimation of the remaining estimates.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> I get really good results on configural and metric, but a big degradation when moving to scalar testing. (So config > CFI.scaled = 0.945; RMSEA.scale = 0.072, then metric > CFI.scaled = 0.941; RMSEA.scaled = 0.072, but then scalar > CFI.scaled = 0.867; RMSEA.scaled = 0.087)

I don't think comparing these fit indices amounts to an omnibus test of invariance.  But assuming (1) metric invariance is at least approximately true, (2) residual variances are also approximately equal, and (3) common-factor variances are also approximately equal, then you could switch to a single-group MIMIC model that regresses the common factors on 6 dummy codes for the 7 countries.  Then estimation is less problematic, and you could look at score tests for the regression of individual indicators (e.g., one at a time) on the 6 dummy codes.  That's 23 omnibus tests, and then estimate paths for significant score tests so you can quantify impact.

>
> As I said, I can't just run lavTestScore() on the whole scalar model as it won't converge, and running it a bit at a time is not practical, so I don't know where to go from here. I am happy to state in my thesis that the MGCFA is configural and metric invariant, but evidence for scalar invariance is lacking. But I want to then regress these latent factors on a dependent variable, and of course without scalar invariance, I fear that is not a sound approach.

Scalar invariance across countries is not required to make valid comparisons of covariance-structure parameters across countries; only metric invariance is required.  Scalar invariance would be required to compare (adjusted-)means/intercepts across countries.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Professor Jorgensen, this is enormously helpful! And I have to say, this sort of information is so elusive on the net; everything I've found has been on the lines of "if no scalar invariance, try to have partial scalar invariance" but with no account of pragmatically what to do if you can't achieve partial scalar invariance.

Your point about making valid comparisons of covariance-structure parameters across countries (but not means/intercepts) - I don't suppose you have a reference for this? Or an example of this being applied in practice to a multi-group dataset?

Thanks
Victoria

On Monday, March 28, 2022 at 2:33:55 PM UTC+1 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I get really good results on configural and metric, but a big degradation when moving to scalar testing. (So config > CFI.scaled = 0.945; RMSEA.scale = 0.072, then metric > CFI.scaled = 0.941; RMSEA.scaled = 0.072, but then scalar > CFI.scaled = 0.867; RMSEA.scaled = 0.087)
>
> I don't think comparing these fit indices amounts to an omnibus test of invariance.  But assuming (1) metric invariance is at least approximately true, (2) residual variances are also approximately equal, and (3) common-factor variances are also approximately equal, then you could switch to a single-group MIMIC model that regresses the common factors on 6 dummy codes for the 7 countries.  Then estimation is less problematic, and you could look at score tests for the regression of individual indicators (e.g., one at a time) on the 6 dummy codes.  That's 23 omnibus tests, and then estimate paths for significant score tests so you can quantify impact.
>
> >
> > As I said, I can't just run lavTestScore() on the whole scalar model as it won't converge, and running it a bit at a time is not practical, so I don't know where to go from here. I am happy to state in my thesis that the MGCFA is configural and metric invariant, but evidence for scalar invariance is lacking. But I want to then regress these latent factors on a dependent variable, and of course without scalar invariance, I fear that is not a sound approach.
>
> Scalar invariance across countries is not required to make valid comparisons of covariance-structure parameters across countries; only metric invariance is required.  Scalar invariance would be required to compare (adjusted-)means/intercepts across countries.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen

> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: Multgroup CFA with ordinal variables: strict and scalar invariance; structural invariance
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am testing multigroup CFA with ordinal variables (three levels, 0,1,2) and testing invariance across three groups.

Based on the Wu and Estabrook article and a few other discussions I have found online, I am using the measEq.syntax to specify configural, metric, scalar and strict invariance models. Configural and metric models had no issue for me. For simplicity, this is the syntax for scalar model that I used:

Model_full_fit_scalar <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = Model_full,
                                       data = dat,
                                       ordered = TRUE,
                                       parameterization = "theta",
                                       ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",
                                       ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                                       group = "grouping",
                                       group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings","intercepts"))
And the strict invariance model only differ by adding "residuals" in group.equal=.

One issue came up: the chi-sq statistics for the strict and scalar model were identical, even though the degrees of freedom were not, and there were slight differences in CFI, and TLI. I have checked the syntax to make sure that the residuals of items were constrained across groups.

How do I interpret the same chi-sq between the two models? Can I interpret the strict model results in this case? Finally, I also intend to test structural invariance (e.g., factor covariances and variances) across groups. Is strict invariance required to test structural invariance?

Happy to provide additional details if needed
Thanks all!!

messages.subject_clean: Multgroup CFA with ordinal variables: strict and scalar invariance; structural invariance
messages.body_plain:
Strict invariance should include more restrictions, so degrees of freedom should be higher. If chi-square does not increase, this indicates that the test was not able to detect discrepancy between the incremental constraints and the data. That failure may be due to a lack of power or due to the additional constraints actually matching the population covariance matrix. The usual statistical test is a chi-square difference test. But if chi-squares are identical--quite surprising, actually--then the chi-square difference is 0, supporting the additional constraints. CFI incorporates the quantity max ( chi-square - degrees of freedom, 0), so if chi-square does not change but degrees of freedom get larger, this quantity will get smaller, as long as chi-square is greater than degrees of freedom.

messages.subject: Re: Multgroup CFA with ordinal variables: strict and scalar invariance; structural invariance
messages.subject_clean: Multgroup CFA with ordinal variables: strict and scalar invariance; structural invariance
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
my collaborators and I had the same problem when we tried to run a multigroup CFA with an ordinal variable with 3 response cateogories (levels).
I sent an email to Ryne Estabrook, since he wrote a very nice article on how to conduct multigroup CFA (Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045).
This is what he texted me back:

"The fact that you’re at three categories (and thus, two thresholds) suggests something to me. Each ordinal item requires two constraints to scale the underlying continuous variable we assume is beneath it. When you constrain your model to have equal thresholds across groups, you’re simply rescaling each variable, which won’t result in any loss of fit. Put differently, there’s no difference in constraining the thresholds for item 1 group 2 to be zero and one or constraining them to be the same as item 1 group 1.
This issue is the broad point of that paper. There’s no such thing as an unconstrained categorical factor model. You make some constraints to make the model identifiable. Sometimes those constraints interact with other constraints in weird ways. You started at something equivalent to the configurally invariant model, so making that “constraint” didn’t change anything".

Indeed, when I tried another CFA with more than 3 response categories I didn't have this issue anymore.

Hope this helps.

Best regards,

Michael Schepisi

messages.subject: Change lavaan syntax dynamically and programmatically with R objects
messages.subject_clean: Change lavaan syntax dynamically and programmatically with R objects
messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to change syntax for a lavaan model dynamically and programmatically with R objects? I’d like to include the contents of an R object in lavaan syntax. As an example, I’d like to fix parameters to a value specified from an R object.

Here is an example:
```
library("lavaan")

sampleSize <- 1000

set.seed(52242)
mydata <- data.frame(matrix(nrow = sampleSize, ncol = 4))
names(mydata) <- c("predictorLatentSEM","criterionLatentSEM","predictorObservedSEM","criterionObservedSEM")

latentCorrelation <- .8
reliabilityPredictor <- .9
reliabilityCriterion <- .85

mydata$predictorLatentSEM <- rnorm(sampleSize, 0 , 1)
mydata$criterionLatentSEM <- latentCorrelation * mydata$predictorLatentSEM + rnorm(sampleSize, 0, sqrt(1 - latentCorrelation ^ 2))
mydata$predictorObservedSEM <- reliabilityPredictor * mydata$predictorLatentSEM + rnorm(sampleSize, 0, sqrt(1 - reliabilityPredictor ^ 2))
mydata$criterionObservedSEM <- reliabilityCriterion * mydata$criterionLatentSEM + rnorm(sampleSize, 0, sqrt(1 - reliabilityCriterion ^ 2))

# This works
model_syntax <- '
# Factor loadings
predictorLatent =~ 1*predictorObservedSEM
criterionLatent =~ 1*criterionObservedSEM

# Factor correlation
criterionLatent ~ predictorLatent

# Residual errors
predictorObservedSEM ~~ (1 - .9^2)*predictorObservedSEM # where .9 is the value of `reliabilityPredictor`
criterionObservedSEM ~~ (1 - .85^2)*criterionObservedSEM # where .85 is the value of `reliabilityCriterion`
'

model_fit <- sem(model_syntax,
data = mydata,
missing = "ML")

# This does not work
model_syntax2 <- '
# Factor loadings
predictorLatent =~ 1*predictorObservedSEM
criterionLatent =~ 1*criterionObservedSEM

# Factor correlation
criterionLatent ~ predictorLatent

# Residual errors
predictorObservedSEM ~~ (1 - reliabilityPredictor^2)*predictorObservedSEM
criterionObservedSEM ~~ (1 - reliabilityCriterion^2)*criterionObservedSEM
'

model_fit2 <- sem(model_syntax2,
data = mydata,
missing = "ML")
```

In the example above, I’d like to fix the residual error of the `predictorObservedSEM` variable to be equal to the value of `(1 - reliabilityPredictor ^ 2)`. However, the lavaan syntax does not seem to allow fixing parameters based on the values from other R objects. In this minimal example, I’m trying to specify a fixed parameter, but It’d be nice to extend this to be able to specify fixed parameters, parameter labels, starting values, which variables load on a factor, etc. programmatically based on the contents of R objects.

Thanks in advance,
Isaac
